utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Due to some technical difficulties, we moved courtroom -- we've moved to Courtroom III and the start of the trial has been delayed for 15 minutes. Yes, where were we? Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I will note that we'll continue to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have 65 ter 11218, and may I have page 37 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I just want to remind you, and myself as well, that we both need to speak rather slowly.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And after you give an answer, I'm going to make a pause so the transcript can catch up with us. Yesterday, when we ended, we were talking about sources that you used in your municipality report. And you mentioned that you used the census from 1991 and that you also used voters' registrations records from 1997. Can you remind us of the number of persons who registered to vote in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The number of registered voters was high. In absolute terms, it was 2.5 million who registered. And it was a high participation rate of almost 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you also tell us how many people registered -- or were registered in the census in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population registered in the census was 4.4 million people.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you do a comparison between the 1991 census and the 1997 voters' registration?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This comparison was done by, first of all, linking all individual records, one record representing one person, and in this way to trace those reported in 1991 in the census in a post-conflict source on surviving population. That is the voters.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what percentage of the records did you find were linked?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was approximately 80 per cent of the voters who registered that were confirmed in the population census.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was this the methodology that you used in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The linking of records is the core of the methodology we used. The linking gives us the possibility to compare pieces of information about the same persons at two different moments of time - in 1991 and in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to talk about that in detail. And on the screen in front of you, you should have Annex C. It's page 226 in Annex C, and this talks about your methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. We don't have the e-court working on our side here, so we're not able to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. All I can see is the documents in private -- or personal computer, but it's not working on the common drive.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am able to cite the page of the report itself. So if everyone has their hard copy, we can still continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you bring the hard copy with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't bring it either. Given the -- Shall we take a short break so that the technicians could look into the matter and fix it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I consult the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber will rise for ten minutes, and hopefully the problem can be solved in that time. We rise for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 9.25 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so we are going to speak now specifically about the methodology which we can see is part of Annex C. Dr. Tabeau, what were the three variables in which you were interested for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interested in place of residence of individuals reported in 1991 census, on one hand, and on the other hand, in a post-war source, that is, voters' register. These were the two of the three variables. And the third variable was ethnicity. Ethnicity as reported in the open-ended question in the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why were you particularly interested in these three variables?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These three variables make it possible to analyse the population movements between these two moments of time, 1991 versus 1997, for every ethnic group separately. When I am saying "every group separately," I mean for every main ethnic group, like Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and all other ethnicities jointly as "others."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You mentioned that in the census in 1991 place where the person lived was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This -- we even have a detailed address for every person, but, as well, we have information about the so-called settlements and larger areas, these are municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In 1997, did the voter registration records specifically indicate where that person lived in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a variable, a self-reported place of residence, but we rather use another variable from the voters' register, this is the place of registration to vote. So this is a very good proxy for the place of residence, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in a general way, can you tell us about the process you employed to figure out which persons were on the 1991 census and were also on the 1997 voters' registration?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, the matching could be done using the unique personal identification number, the JMBG, as the same people reported in the census and in the voters' register had the same unique number. So this was the first step in our matching process. Of course, there was a group of records with -- for which it wasn't achieved for various reasons, so in the next step we did our matching using descriptive data items, such as names - first, father's name, surname - date of birth, place of birth. This matching is more complex than the first type. The first is based on one numeric data item. It's very, very easy to do this kind of matching. Names are more complex. Still, a lot of success can be achieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now once you had a set of linked records, what did that tell you about the identified people?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These matched records was the group for -- of whom we had a lot of information for both years, for 1991 and 1997. Basically we were interested in comparing places of residence in both these years, and ethnicity. So having these lots of information, we selected three variables and studied in order to compile statistics as the ones presented in the municipalities report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let me ask you some questions about that. Did the linking, the successful link, tell you that the person survived the war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did the successful link tell you what the ethnicity of the person was?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did it tell you where they lived in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did it also tell you where they registered to vote in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the significance for you of a person who lived in one place in 1991 but lived in a different place in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an indication of a movement which we considered to be a displacement compared with the original 1991 place of residence. So basically we used a statistical definition to decide whether a person can be considered a displaced person or a refugee, or the person didn't move.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned earlier in your testimony that there were groups of individuals who were not included in the 1997 registration. You said that these were people who didn't want to register, some maybe too old, too ill, and others perhaps too young. Was anyone who was born in 1980 and afterwards included in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This the first criterion to -- for being eligible to vote. It is the age criteria. Those who are eligible have to be 18 years of age at time of elections. So these people who were born after 1980 plus other later years are not part of the voters' register.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as a result of that, did that make your numbers larger or smaller?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course smaller, because obviously also among children below 18 years of age they were displaced persons who obviously moved with their parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This methodology that you've spoken about and these sources, are these all included in the annex that we see on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender 65 ter 11218. This is the annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many reports, expert reports, are you going to tender through Dr. Tabeau, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's a total of six. For the municipalities, there's just one plus this annex that you see. For the Sarajevo portion of the case, there are three. And for the Srebrenica portion, there are two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In total, 11 items.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think the extra items are just addendums to some of the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you are tendering them as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any objections to the admission of any of those items?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They are all admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall I -- the exhibit number will be informed by the Registrar in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 10723; e-court page 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, we're now going to talk about estimates, statistical estimates, that you made in regard to these reports. Before we do so, I'd like to look at your report, the Mr. Karadzic report on municipalities, to review how it's divided. First off, in 1991 how many municipalities were in the BiH?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: After the war ended, how many municipalities were there?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: 189 codes were assigned to municipal areas, but a number of these codes were empty. So in total it was 149.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Why were there more after than before the war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is because of how the country changed during the war. The Dayton line actually split a number of municipalities in two areas, one belonging to Republika Srpska and one to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the main reason. But there were also a low number of new municipalities, very small areas cut off from the old municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you able to account for the split in your results?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We analysed municipalities as available from the post-Dayton classification, official classification, which number is higher than the pre-war municipalities number.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, the annex to your report, this is what we see on the screen, Annex A, is lengthy, and I just want to go through it briefly. This covers your results for internally displaced persons for all the 27 municipalities relevant in this indictment. In regards to Table 1, can you tell us what's included in Table 1?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Table 1 reports on the changes in the ethnic composition. There is the population size in 1991 and of the complete population and the size of the sample population from the voters' register, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you noted earlier that ethnicities were reported in the 1991 census. How many ethnicities did you include in your tables?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all tables, only four major groups are included. The category "others" comprises the remaining category different than Serbs, Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So we have a total of four. Does that mean there are four tables for each municipality in this annex?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each ethnic group has a separate table. So ethnic -- change in the ethnic composition is reported separately for Muslims, Serbs, Croats, others, and each of these tables will be listing all the 27 municipalities included in the indictment of this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, for the record, that's e-court pages 0964 through 0975.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now let's go to Table 2. Can you tell us what Table 2 regards?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Table 2 presents the minimum number of internally displaced persons and refugees obtained from our linking methodology. These are minimum numbers, which means only the numbers that were obtained from the matched records of voters backed with the census. They are called, therefore, minimum, as the voters' register is a sample, very large, but sample, so we have the minimum number. They can be documented with lists of all these displaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Again, is this four tables as well for each municipality for all 27 -- excuse me, for each ethnicity for all 27 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For the record it's e-court page 0976 to 0987.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can look at Table 3. Tell us what those tables regard.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Table --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I would ask the Prosecutor if there is going to be any kind of redactions to reflect that 20 municipalities are charged pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision under Rule 73 bis (D) as opposed to the 27 that were charged at the time she did her analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand the elimination of those seven, but I do believe, like your observations about evidence on Zepa, the information on those other seven do still go to the overarching JCE, and I would include them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then we can calculate on our own based upon the tables that follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct. So it's easy to take out the seven municipalities because the tables are split up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, our position is that the Chamber shouldn't consider any evidence with respect to the seven municipalities which have been stricken. You ordered the Prosecution not to lead evidence of the seven municipalities. And in the municipalities portion of the case, we have had rulings by the Chamber with respect to Brcko and possibly another municipality where you found that the material of the 20 municipalities that were before you were sufficient and that it was not necessary in this component of the case to receive evidence of other municipalities to show a pattern. So, consistent with that ruling, I don't believe that the Court should consider any of the seven municipalities that have been stricken from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, as a matter of practicality, I don't think it's necessary, absolutely necessary, to ask the doctor to calculate again, as long as we can do it on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you leave it in the hands of the Chamber later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, tell us about Table 3.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Table 3 is a sort of follow-up on Table 2. It presents a more complete number of internally displaced persons and refugees. The more complete number could be obtained as an estimate. It is a number that is produced using standard statistical techniques for estimation of unknown numbers of certain events in the population. And this estimated number of internally displaced persons and refugees is presented in Table 3. As with any estimates, statistical estimates, also some uncertainty around this number is expressed in this table.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the term "refugee." Can you tell us what the statistical definition is of "refugee"?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a refugee is a person who left his or her home and moved to another country different than Bosnia and Herzegovina. Unlike the definition of the internally displaced person who moved only within Bosnia-Herzegovina and didn't go to another country.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you understand there to be a legal definition of "refugee" that is different than the statistical definition?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I am aware of such definition. And, as a matter of fact, what we discussed yesterday, among sources we had this one source called DDPR, which is the official register of internally displaced persons and refugee in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Official register was made by UNHCR together with local authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this data, this source, represents IDPs and refugees as presented according to the legal definition of a refugee and an internally displaced person, but cross-referencing this with our statistics, I can say there is a huge consistency between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And lastly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, going back to the issue that Mr. Robinson raised just now, just in case, i.e., for the -- purely for the reference of the Chamber, I would like to produce the separate table, or number or numbers or ratio, in consultation with Dr. Tabeau after her evidence is over that would include the municipalities that have been taken out from the indictment, but not now. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, looking at the last portion of the tables, Tables 1 BH, 2 BH, 3 BH, tell us about those.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These three tables are exactly the same as Table 1, 2, and 3, only that they are presenting one large area, Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a whole, for just reference purposes, no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this includes all the municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it includes all municipalities in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The findings that you made in the table, are those findings also conveyed in writing elsewhere in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Findings presented very specifically in a detailed way in the Annex A are discussed more generally in the body text of the report. Again, separately for every ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I do not want to go through all these tables, but I think the best way to convey this information is by giving one example. And you've prepared a handout showing one example; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 23719. And for the parties, this is the handout that has been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is titled as "courtroom presentation."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll go to page 1 of that. Tell us what the source of the material was for this handout.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This comes from my report from Tables 1, 2, 3 in the annex. Annex A, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we see now Table 1, and this specifically regards Prijedor; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, going across the rows, we see at the top that you have the ethnicities. And then you have 1991 and a number of -- numbers follow. What are those?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this table generally reports on the change in the ethnic composition between 1991 and 1997. Numbers in the first part of the table under 1991 and 1997 are just absolute numbers of those individuals based -- for whom we study this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say absolute numbers, when we look at row 1991, are those the actual numbers reported by the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So, for instance, for all ethnicities, there were 94.028 individuals that were born before 1980 reported in the census.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then we look at 1997, that row, are those the actual absolute numbers reported from the voters' registration?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. This is the sample of registered voters linked back with the records of the population census.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now let's go down to the percentage section and the 1991 row. Is that the percentages those ethnicities made up in the entire population of the country in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this example is just for one municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we are discussing the municipality of Prijedor in this example. Indeed in the second part of the table our reading should go in rows. In the first row there is the ethnic composition expressed in percentages for those living in the municipality of Prijedor. And in the second row, there is ethnic composition, again in relative terms, in percentages, for 1997. These are comparable figures because of the relative nature, unlike the absolute numbers, because here there is a problem that one -- 1991 is representing a complete population, and 1997 is a sample. So comparisons are always possible and meaningful if we look at the percentages. The percentages represent very well the entire population in both cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at what happened to the Serb population in Prijedor from 1991 to 1997.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb population increased or the share of Serbs in the municipality of Prijedor increased from 43.4 per cent in 1991 to 89 per cent in 1997. It is an increase of more than 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at what happened to the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The share of Muslims in 1991 in Prijedor was 42.6 per cent, and in 1997, just 1 per cent. It is a very significant decrease by 97.6 per cent. That is the reading, how these numbers should be looked at in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now let's move to Figure 1. Is this just a visualisation of what those numbers would look like?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are exactly same numbers as in Table 1 presented graphically in Figure 1. The colours, red is associated with the Serbs, and the green, Muslims. These are the two groups, major groups, we have just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we move to Table 2, this is the overall number of IDPs and refugees in Prijedor. Is this table comprised of information from several of the tables in your annex?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most importantly, this table reports on population displacement. But there are pieces of information from all three tables in Annex A, one -- Table 1, Table 2, and 3 put next to each other and making the story more complete than just if you read it table by table.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you go over the column labels and tell us which each of them mean?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, first column is self-explanatory. It is just ethnic groups listed. The next one reports on the 1991 census population. Of course, those born before 1980. Perhaps a short explanation, that we work with this segment of the population is because we want to compare the comparable, that means the same segments in both years, 1991 and 1997, and we don't want to mix up the whole population which is generally available from 1991 census with a sample of ages 18-plus of the eligible voters. Well, going back to the table, so 1991 is included -- 1991 census is included for reference purposes. So, next column, the second column, is giving us the minimum number of internally displaced persons and refugees in Prijedor, or, rather, from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you say "minimum number," is this the number that you actually counted from the 1997 voters' registration?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct. It's the minimum number. Those records matched back with the census for whom we were able to compare the place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the next column is an estimate.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How did you get to that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This estimate is based on a sample proportion of IDPs and refugees, that is, the displaced people. In the voters's sample, this fraction is, in statistical terms, a sampling proportion. We take this proportion and apply it to the exposed population, that is, the 1991 census, and in this way we produce an estimate which is -- which should be seen as some kind of producing a more complete number, like an extrapolation of the sample results over the complete population. That's the estimate, estimated number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, doctor confirmed that all these numbers were taken from the tables that exist in her report. For example, sixty -- no, 642. So as far as this table is concerned, this Table 2, so with the specific numbers, I'd like to be shown each table that shows the number here. For example, where can we see 642? Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I think Dr. Tabeau has indicated that for you on the smaller table below the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, maybe you can tell us about the smaller table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

For a majority of them, it is easily possible because I do it using the JMBG, the unique identification number. So, in the next step, I improve it by running a number of additional criteria to match as many as possible. Once I am done with the matching, for every person who is connected between these two tables, I can look at the full record of information and compare many things, including the place of residence. So if I take one row from Table A and one row from Table B, Table A being 1991 census, Table B being the 1997 voters' register, and I look at Mr. Whoever, Cekic, for example, I look and compare his first name, father's name, surname, date of birth, and place where, on one hand, he lived in 1991 and where he registered to vote in 1997. So I create a data item, a variable, which tells me for every linked person what happened, whether he or she moved or not. So once I'm done with this kind of flagging of records, then I move to the next step. I make my only tabulation of the marking of displacement. And, of course, I also have information about persons, about their ethnicity and age and many, many other things. utterances.text: Serbs, yes, it is correct, line 14, it is Prijedor. We go to the second column for Prijedor. There is a number there, 40.822. 40.822. This is --

utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Tabeau. I'm looking on the screen. At line 14 for Prijedor I see 40.825.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. 25, yes. I was seeing 25 but, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So 40.825. So this is the 1991 census population of Serbs from Prijedor. Of course, it is only those who were born before 1980. Otherwise, I could not compare this number with what I have in the voters' register. So 40.825, I multiply this number by 2.7 per cent, that is my sampling proportion of displaced Serbs from Prijedor. In result of this multiplication, we see the number 1.089 in Table 3, of course, and in our presentation under the estimated number of displaced Serbs from Prijedor ... if we go to the presentation, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 65 ter 23719, e-court page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Table 2, at the bottom of the page. For Serbs, estimated number of IDPs and refugees is 1.089. That is how the method works. So for any other ethnic group, the sampling proportions are different, and in result -- and, of course, the 1991 census populations for each ethnic group are different, the size of them. So this results in the numbers listed as estimated numbers in this third column, and the total of which for all ethnic groups is 45.688. That is the estimated more complete number of displaced persons and refugees from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We see here -- I'm coming back to the number of 40.825 who lived in Prijedor in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And those are Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So bearing that in mind, could we go back to the page 52 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: ERN 09--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm coming back to page 51.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 0986, please. ERN page 0986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Here, total population identified in 1997 who lived in Prijedor in 1991 was 49.019. How -- could you tell us the difference between these two numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number 40.825, these are 1991 Serbs, should be compared with the number 24.070 from Table 2S, page 51. So you mentioned, Your Honour, the number 49.000 from this table. 49.019. Which is a larger number because it covers all ethnicities. If we want the Serbs, to compare with the Serbs, then we have to move to the right in this table and look at the number 24.070. 24.070 is a sample of those 40.825. It's a sample, a large sample, very large sample, from those reported in the census, and I use this sample to produce the more complete number of displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then if you could tell us again the meaning of 40.825.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 40.825 is the number of Serbs listed in 1991 census for Prijedor, and they were born before 1980.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 24.070 is a sample of those Serbs listed in the census in Prijedor who were, as well, identified as voters registered in 1997 elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, first, 4.4 million versus 2.5 million?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is very correct, yes. And linking persons, the same -- the same, very same persons in both years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we can go back to the handout, so it's 23719, e-court page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've -- we were just looking at the Serbs estimated number 1.089. Now, if we continue along that row, we see 95 per cent confidence interval. Dr. Tabeau, is this a type of statistical error that you're accounting for?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This estimated number is a point estimate. Point estimates don't tell us with a certainty about what we estimate. They tell us with a certainty probability or confidence that this unknown estimated number would be equal, what is shown in Table 2. In this particular case, the confidence interval expresses the range of uncertainty, assuming 5 per cent error of the estimation. So if we go to Serbs and look at the estimated number 1.089 and the numbers -- two numbers next to it, the first one is 1.036, the second one is 1.142, so you can see that point estimate is somewhat there between these two values, lower end and upper end of this interval, and the interval itself gives us the 95 per cent confidence that our value is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we'll go to the last two columns. You've got a minimum number percentage and an estimated number percentage. Tell us about those two columns.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is that in these columns some numbers from this particular table are related to each other. A simple calculation of minimum number divided by the 1991 population is reported under 1.6 per cent. That is the share of the minimum number of displaced in the 1991 census population. And next to it, we see the familiar 2.7 per cent. That is the number that relates the estimated unknown number of displacement to the 1991 population.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, I'm not going to go through the Muslim numbers with you, but just like the estimate we gave for the Serbs in Prijedor who were displaced as 1.089, what is the estimate you give for the Muslims from Prijedor that were displaced?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the number of displaced Muslims from Table 2 is 1900 -- sorry, 19.290. That is the second row, second column.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's the minimum absolute number; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the minimum absolute number.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What's the estimate?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The estimate is 39.322.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I now want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And finally, that may be a matter of course, when discussing the person -- internally displaced persons, the reason for such displacement was not looked into. Whether they were forced or they voluntarily moved, you didn't look into such matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Causes -- causes of displacement are not looked at at this -- in this report. It is just measurement of displacement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now, Doctor, I'd like to talk about -- we just talked about Prijedor in particular. Now I would like to talk about the overall number in the 27 municipalities. If we can go to the next page of the handout, and we're going to look at the bottom table, Table 4, which is the same table we just looked at for Prijedor, but this accounts for all 27. And, here, let's focus on the Muslim line going across. So if we start at 481.109, tell us what that represents.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 1991 census count of Muslims in the 27 municipalities of the Karadzic case area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then the 161.047, what number does that -- what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number represents the number of -- minimum number of displaced Muslims from these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was the estimate you came up with, using a sampling proportion for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is 284.239. That is the estimated more complete number of displaced Muslims from these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, the President just asked you whether you analysed the causes of their displacement, and, of course, your answer to that was no. But could you analyse the timing of their displacement, what time between 1991 and 1997 these people moved out?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not easy to analyse the timing because generally sources reporting on timing are not available. However, we were able to find a few sources reporting on early 1993 and later early 1995 which we could use to compare our numbers with.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page of the handout. This will be page 4 in e-court. See on top it says Table 2, population change in some municipalities? And here we see the table begins separated into ethnicities. It begins in 1991. It ends in 1997. But in the middle we have the years 1993 and 1995. What sources did you consult to get informations [sic] from 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two sources were compiled by authorities of Republika Srpska, specifically by the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, in the course -- during the conflict, actually. These are relatively brief sources that cannot be seen comparable with population census made by statistical authorities, yet they report approximate numbers that are very useful for our purposes to compare with our statistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here we only see a listing of nine municipalities. Why are there only nine and not 27?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is because of the specificity of these sources. They only covered the so-called Banja Luka region, which is different generally than the 27 municipalities studied here. However, there is a number of municipalities, specifically nine, that overlap with -- between the two sources, the two types of sources: our and RS sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we will focus particularly on the Muslim table on top. And since we just spoke about Prijedor, let's look at Prijedor again. And, here, for Prijedor, in the column that says 1993 "(moved out)," we have 42.000. What does that number represent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the approximate number of Muslims from Prijedor that are reported here by RS sources as gone, moved out from this municipality, as of early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then, for the column 1995, it says "(residents)" for Prijedor, 3.600. What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number represents the Muslims registered still by RS sources still in the municipality of Prijedor. It would be 3.600 out of 1991 population reported here for Prijedor as 49.351.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so in regard to timing, what was your conclusion as to when the Muslims in Prijedor moved away?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, already by early 1993, a large number of Muslims from Prijedor is reported by independent sources as moved out. So that is a good indication of the timing when people were moving and becoming displaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: These blue boxes we see on these two tables, do these just indicate corrections you made to your report since the last time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a mistake for Sanski Most that has been corrected, and this is highlighted blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page, please, of the handout --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are on this page --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- can you take the table at the bottom of the page which refers to Serbs, which should be C, and not B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Here, in Prijedor, we see the number 47.581 in 1991. Did we see this number before while looking at various tables related to the Prijedor and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we couldn't see this number because this number includes all ages of Prijedor population. That means all those, disregarding when they were born. In our analysis, in previously seen tables, we looked at a segment, a large one, but a segment of population, of all those who, later on in 1997, became 18 years of age and could vote and register. So our population, 1991 population, is obviously smaller than what is reported in this table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page of the handout.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here we see two graphs, Figure 14 and 15. Are these just visualisations of what we saw on the previous page?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the same numbers as on the previous page. Figure 14 represents Muslims. Figure 15, Serbs. What is shown in these two figures is the population in 1991 versus 1995. So the dark brown bars represent 1991. Green ones, 1995. For both. And a per cent is shown instead of absolute numbers, as per cent is a measure that can be easily compared. For Muslims, the pattern clearly indicates that in 1995 the fractions were extremely low compared with 1991, which just further confirms what we studied and obtained in our report. And Figure 15 shows the opposite. The fractions of Serbs increased considerably in 1995 compared to 1991, and, again, the same result was obtained in our report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Tabeau. On the following page of the handout, you did a similar analysis of the Srebrenica municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is an analysis for IDPs, internally displaced people, not for killed people; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is displacement, not killed people.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in this analysis did you apply the same methodology that we talked about for the Prijedor numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the same methodology and the same sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I would now like to move --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to move now to the Sarajevo reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are moving, I have to -- I'd like to note that we passed a number of Prosecution Exhibit 5000. 65 ter 12133 has the honour to have the number P -- Exhibit P5000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Our congratulations to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My congratulations to Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm the lucky person.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we'll move on to Sarajevo. Can you tell us - you've been at the OTP for several years - what was the first study that you did regarding the events of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chronologically the first report I made was for Galic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And that Galic report was for the period of time September 1992 to August 1994. Was that the period of time when Galic was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the next report that you did on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next one was for the case of Dragomir Milosevic. And the coverage was September 1994 to November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right. And was that the period of time where Dragomir Milosevic was then the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the last report that you wrote for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last report I made for this case, for the Karadzic case, and it covers the first five months of the siege. That is, from April 1995 to 9 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would that be April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Of course, 1992. Yes. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the Karadzic report covers the period of time not covered by Galic and the Milosevic reports?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These reports are exclusive. So three of them covered the entire period from April 1992 to November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And we will talk about all three. And we're going to do it chronologically. But first I want to ask you: What was your task for all of these reports?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was to come up with a number, reliable number, of victims of the siege, both civilian victims and military victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for each of these three reports, did you use the same methodology?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two of these reports were based on the same methodology and the same sources, and the third one, the Dragomir Milosevic report, was slightly different, still within the standard methodology used throughout the years here in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 12130, please. 12130, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Doctor, this is your report for this case. It's April 1992 to September of 1992. What area, what geographical area, does this report cover?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area covered in this report is the so-called within-front-lines area of Sarajevo. In terms of municipalities, this within-front area covers large parts of six urban municipalities of Sarajevo, and they are all listed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the main source you used in preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main source used to compile statistics, again, minimum numbers, on killed persons and wounded person was the so-called Sarajevo household survey. This is a large survey conducted in Sarajevo by local researchers by mid-1994. So the front -- within-the-front-lines area should be seen as the area that was located inside the front lines as of this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we will speak in detail about the survey in a moment. But were there other sources that you consulted peripherally as well?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There was another source reporting on that, the so-called Bakije funeral home, the largest and the oldest funeral home of Sarajevo that was burying the Muslim population, exclusively Muslims. Well, we used this source mainly to produce an estimate of a more complete number of victims. This source is not used to compile statistics on killed and wounded population. We also used another source, the 1991 population census, which we actually always use when working on victims in order, first of all, to validate the -- the information about persons listed in a source on victims with how the same person is reported in the census, that is, the validation of victim records and possibly improving them using the census population information. And secondly, we used the census in order to acquire the ethnicity of victims. We always use this one definition of ethnicity based on the open-ended question from the 1991 population census. In addition to the census, we also used military lists of all three armies that were engaged in combat in Bosnia, and these lists were used to give us information about who can be considered a military person, a soldier, and who, a civilian. In this particular case, in Sarajevo household survey, the civilian military status was, however, also available from our main source.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So we are going to talk about the main source, this household survey. And, for the record, you wrote in detail about this in your Galic report, starting at page 10. We don't need to go there. But can you tell us when the household survey of Sarajevo was conducted?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was conducted in mid-1994, as far as I remember, from April to August, or even early September of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And who conducted it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group who conducted it and designed the questionnaire were researchers from the Institute for War Crimes and International Law in Sarajevo. They were able to develop this questionnaire in this difficult time for the importance of this survey to everybody, and also with a lot of assistance from the statistical authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What area was covered by the survey?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, the area was within the front lines, six urban municipalities, large parts of these municipalities. Obviously the number of individuals and households included in this survey must have been high, and it was. It was a large number of 85.000 households that were interviewed in this survey. 85.000 households are equivalent to approximately 340.000 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And you said there was interviews. Were they face-to-face interviews?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were face-to-face interviews conducted by a group of interviewers that were trained and instructed how to question the households in this survey.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You just mentioned that it was 85.000 households equivalent to approximately 340.000 individuals. How do you know it was 340.000 individuals?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an approximate number. The exact number, I don't know, and I don't know because this huge massive material has never been computerised in whole. Only the part that was needed for our work was computerised, and yet it was a lot of work at that time. This number 340.000 individuals is an estimation based on the assumption that the average size of one household is four persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Prior to the war, did you know what the average size of a household was?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was smaller than four persons. It was three-something. There is a footnote in my report which tells the exact number, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Why did you increase that number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I increased that number because there were newcomers to Sarajevo who were staying with their families who originally lived in the Sarajevo area, so that is one reason. And in the Galic report, we also calculated demographic rates, that is, the relative measures of killing and wounding. And if we would keep the population size small, this would affect the rates by increasing them, and we don't want to do that. We rather keep the rates conservative. That means we rather include more population at risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned -- I think you mentioned there was a questionnaire. And the actual questionnaire is in the annex to the Karadzic report. But can you tell us in particular the questions in which you were interested?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were questions related to whether there were family members killed during the war in this given family, whether there were persons wounded, whether there were natural deaths. I think these were the three major questions that I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And once the interviews were done -- strike that. The process of computerising and screening all this information, was that a process that you yourself were involved?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We actually didn't even try to request a database from the institute who -- who made this survey because they didn't have one. What they had were the original questionnaires. The questionnaires needed to be computerised and processed, and this is what I was in charge of and in which I was involved with some other colleagues from my unit. So we actually selected a sample of original questionnaires and copied them and arranged data entry, and all this was done as our project, as the Demographic Unit project.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And out of the 85.000 household questionnaires, how many did you take?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 40.000. This is the number of questionnaires that reported either on killing or on wounding in the family, or on natural deaths, or combinations thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And the remaining -- the other 45.000, they didn't have information in which you were interested; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've already spoken about the matching or the linking process. Was that the same process used here?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the standard procedure, matching procedure, as in other projects.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the 40.000 questionnaires that you had, did you match them to the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them. There is a high matching rate though, more than 81 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: By doing so for the 81 per cent, did you become aware of how that 81 per cent reported their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Through the links, we could learn about how they reported themselves in the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to the handout number 23719, looking for e-court page 7, please. So it will be number -- page 6 in the handout. This is a table on the Karadzic Sarajevo report that we have put in the handout, and this is from page 4 and 5 of the report. Now, I'd like to look at some of the results that you came up with. And here we see Table 1, an overview of the summary statistics from the household survey. We see under variables, the column labelled "variables," sample size. Tell us what you mean here by sample size.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sample size should be understood here as a selection of cases, of records, from the overall computerised Sarajevo household survey questionnaires. The sample size should be seen as the size of victims population. Records were selected based on the relevance to this particular indictment period, which is April 1992 to 9 September 1992, so only these records were selected that were falling within this time-frame. So under the sample size in the second column, there is the overall total. And under the column "killed," there is a number reported. 2.028 is the number. And that's the number, a minimum number, of killed persons selected because of the relevance to this particular indictment period. All these cases of killing took place within the front lines of Sarajevo as of mid-1994. And the next number, absolute number, in the second-last column, is 7.374. I repeat the number: 7.374. This is the number of wounded persons from the same territory and the same time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And included on the questionnaire was information that the person killed or wounded was a civilian or a soldier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an indication of the civilian/military status.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And in addition, in describing the event that caused the killing or the wounding, what type of information was included?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information about the year of birth, which made it possible for us to study ages of those killed and wounded, and most importantly we also had information about the cause of killing and wounding, a cause that we were able to process according to categories such as shelling, sniping, fire-arms, other fire-arms, and a number of additional other causes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And that information is at the bottom of this table; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The second table we see, here you just took out the civilians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we turn now to the next page of the handout - page 7 in the handout, page 8 in e-court - this regards causes of death and causes of -- cause of wounding. And here we see five particular categories. Can you tell the Chamber how it is that you organised these five categories?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The causes were reported by respondents without any instructions or standardisation of categories. People reported causes as they knew them. So my task was to study these reports and to come up with a meaningful classification that could be done in such a way that every cause would be reported in a consistent way. During our process of standardisation, we kept the originally reported categories as often as possible. So what see -- what we can see under fire-arms, shelling, sniping, general shooting, are categories that were originally reported by the respondents.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I just want to focus on that category of fire-arms. On the column to the extreme right on each table, you have a percentage.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you add up the percentages on the first table, Table 2, for fire-arms, so we begin with 59.7 per cent, 14.1 per cent --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- and down to 5.1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- what is the total percentages of deaths caused by fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is 88.4 per cent, which is a very large per cent of all causes reported by respondents.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, that's for people killed. Now, if we move over and go to wounded people and do the same thing and add up the percentages for fire-arms, what is the total per cent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This per cent is even higher, and it is equal, 96.8 per cent. Almost 97 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So far, in this report, the numbers we have spoken about are minimum numbers. They're direct, actual numbers that you yourself counted. Were you able to translate these numbers into actual estimates of people killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The numbers which are included in Table 1 are minimum numbers. They are minimum numbers because even though our source was very large and reliable, still it is not that one source can report all victims of war. This is not how the experience shows us things are done during conflict. So it is certain that Sarajevo household survey is not a complete source. The estimation that we made included two sources: One is the Sarajevo household survey, and the second one is the Bakije funeral home.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So in order to give an overall estimate of numbers of killed and wounded in Sarajevo in this time-frame, what statistical tool did you use?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used a simple method which is used particularly for this type of estimation, the method called capture/recapture.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And with this method, does it require one independent source or two?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This method requires at least two independent sources. It is possible to have three, if exists. In our case, we had two sources, independent sources, at our disposal, so capture/recapture estimation was completed based on two.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, one of those sources we have already spoken about in detail, and that's the household survey report. And the second source you mentioned was the Bakije funeral home records. Can you tell us a little bit more about that source?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bakije funeral home is a Muslim funeral home. That means from this source we have information about deaths of Muslims exclusively. And the number for the entire war period reported in this source is approximately 12 -- more than 12.000, which compares with other sources, like Sarajevo household survey. Only that this is just one ethnic group, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And these records cover a time-frame that is bigger than the time-frame for this report; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But information about dates of funeral, which are very close to the dates of death, we can extract the relevant records for our purpose, for our estimation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you've already mentioned the statistical tool called capture/recapture. In a very general way, can you explain to us what that is?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. One more remark about the Bakije funeral home. It covers both killings and natural deaths. It's one important starting point for how we applied the capture/recapture. Capture/recapture is a method that was originally developed to estimate the size of wild populations that cannot be easily measured. If we think of fish, for instance, then it is not possible to go to the ocean and then count them all. In such cases, samples are taken of fish from the sea and compared, cross-referenced. And based on this, estimation can be made which provides us with unknown total. The same method was applied to human populations, like, for instance, HIV patients who are also counted with huge difficulties, were estimated in various studies using capture/recapture. The method is based on a simple assumption, that the overlap between two samples is a meaningful piece of information that can take us to produce the unknown overall size of population. Well, in order -- in common language: If we have a sample taken from a population, larger population, if we mark individuals selected for the sample and let them go to mix up with the rest of the population, would be the first step in capture/recapture. In the second step, a second sample is drawn, and we check how many individuals in the second sample have been marked as also present previously in the first sample. The individuals checked to be first in the first sample and overlap with the second sample is the overlap of the two samples. The method is based on a simple assumption, that the proportion of the first sample size to the unknown population size is exactly the same as the proportion of recaptured individuals to the size of the sample 2. So we have two proportions. One proportion illustrating the recaptures individual -- individuals, in sample 2, in relation to the size of this sample, and the other proportion is the entire sample 1 to the unknown population --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- size.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- if you apply that proportion to the entire population, is that how you get your estimate?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed. This is, again, like extrapolation of sampling proportion in order to estimate the unknown overall population size. The details of this method are described in the report in Annex --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The details of this are in the Karadzic report, page 30 and 58.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the handout, please. So what we'll see here is Table 12 where you applied that estimation. And we see that it's split up into ethnicities for this period of time in 1992 in this particular geographical location. Under "observed," we see Croat, 53. What does "observed" mean?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are exactly same numbers as those reported in Table 1. So the overall total in Table 12 is 2.028, and it's exactly the same as the overall number of killed in Table 1. So observed are the counts based on Sarajevo household survey. Ethnicity comes from links of victim records with the 1991 census. There is a small category of unknowns, 470; for those we don't have ethnicity, as they are unmatched.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So the ethnicity that you reported here, this is -- is this how these people reported themselves in the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when we go from 53 Croats observed to the estimated 80, to get that number, did you apply the capture/recapture theory?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the method it was applied is rather complex, because, as I mentioned, the funeral home, Bakije does only include information about Muslims. Moreover, it includes both killings and natural deaths. So capture/recapture was in the first step applied to the Muslim population exclusively. Muslims, both killings and natural deaths, as reported in both sources. So overlap was studied only for Muslims, both killed and natural deaths, in both sources. Applying capture/recapture to one category is not complex mathematically and statistically. So once this was done, in the next step we extrapolated these results. First we split the estimate between killings and natural deaths. And further, when looking exclusively at killings and saw how much Muslim killed population increased from capture/recapture results, once this was finished, we applied the same degree of increase to every other ethnic group. So the method was applied in several steps, in three steps. Basically what we present here in Table 12 are relevant, 100 per cent relevant, results related to killings only and to the time-frame of indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West. So let's take the example of Muslims, which we see in this Table 12. So could -- could the doctor explain us how 1.811 number could be reached using that capture and recapture estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, of course. I suggest we move to the annex from the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Doctor, would that be Annex 6?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 59.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 12130. ERN ending in 8525. It's almost the end of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second-last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we could please take a look at Table A6.1 in the middle of this page. This table summarises the input data used for the estimation. We have numbers of both killed persons and natural deaths shown as available from the two sources. First one, HSS 1994, is the Household Survey Sarajevo. In this source, the number of killed Muslims and natural deaths of Muslims equals 1.707. The number of the same type of deaths reported in the Bakije funeral home is 1.576. From the matching of the two sources at the individual record level, we obtain the overlap between these two sources. The overlap means these are cases reported in both sources. This number, overlap, is 1.039. If we go down, there is a formula which tells us the capital N with a hat, which is the unknown size of the population that we estimate, can be obtained from a simple operation which multiplies Sample 1 by Sample 2 and divides this multiplication by the overlap. From this formula we obtain the number reported in the last paragraph at the bottom, which says N-hat equals 2589.251. This number, 2.589, approximately, is the estimated number of both killed Muslims and natural deaths of Muslims. That is the first step of our capture/recapture estimation. Starting from here, we apply the proportion of killings and natural deaths as obtained from Sarajevo household survey and distribute this number into two categories. And one portion obtained from the proportion of killings in Sarajevo household survey gives us the number, estimated number, in 12 -- in Table 12, which equals 1.811.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just -- just a second. I have to admit that this is beyond my capability. Mr. Robinson, do you challenge this formula which is related to this purely the capture/recapture method, scientifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to defer this to Dr. Karadzic because he's been working with our expert who doesn't speak English, so I myself don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, the sample with plants and animals in an ocean, where it's impossible to have a different register, is absolutely not applicable to a civilised environment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm not asking you as to the applicability of this formula to the Sarajevo case. But my question is whether you challenge this formula itself when it applies to wild animal or whatever. Otherwise I have to ask the doctor to explain in more detail so that layman could understand. Or give us some examples of this method. If you do not challenge this formula as such, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I challenge the formula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if you do so, it will be noted that your expert is challenging this formula itself. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Tabeau, you have heard that Dr. Karadzic is challenging the formula. Would it be possible for you to give it to us in a more simplified form so that it could be a little more easily digested? Is it possible at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Honestly, I thought I was giving it in a very simple form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Where you really?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought I were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So to think of an even simpler example is hard, but I can prepare something. I can do my best and come up with a very simple example, because, yes, it is a simple method which is based on equality of two proportions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But we shall be grateful for that even more simplified form.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Extremely grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, yes. One more remark, if I may. It is not that I invented it. It is that I have references for the authors and applications. And it is not what -- that I'm telling that I came up with this formula and all kinds of things like, you know, error estimation and stuff. There is a huge literature on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: We weren't implying that at all. We weren't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make a suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has a meeting, some internal meeting at 12.30, so I was about to suggest to adjourn now for a break. And then can I hear your suggestion, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My suggestion was going to be that Dr. Tabeau is going to have to come back another day. And if we could hold off on this example so she can give us a meaningful thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- maybe we could address it on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And were the parties informed that on Tuesday we'll start at 11.00 in light of the fact that the accused will have an interview with a certain witness I don't know? We'll rise for the break and we'll resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.21 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to make three corrections to the transcript: Page 9, line 19, it should be "Muslims" and not "multiples." Page 13, line 6, it should be "Annex A," not "Annex C." Page 39, line 11, it should be "causes," not "cautions."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, when we finished at the last session, we were talking about estimates. And now I want to move on to another part of this report that regards timing. This is another area that you analysed. It was the timing of civilian deaths per day versus soldiers killed per day. Can you tell us what the purpose was of this particular analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The analysis of timing has the purpose to investigate the siege intensity. This can be done when analysing the timing of killings and woundings of soldiers. And in addition to this, the purpose was to investigate what was the timing of killings and wounding of civilians. Whether these two timings were consistently the same or different. Whether the numbers of killed civilians were the same, higher, or lower compared with the numbers of killed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Before we go into the results in detail, can you just tell us in general what you found?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
