utterances.text: Generally, the starting point for this analysis was that when we look at timing of killings or woundings of civilians in relation to timing obtained for soldiers, that the killings of civilians should be insignificantly -- insignificant compared with the numbers of soldiers. If there are combat activities, our assumption was that in combat soldiers are killed or wounded, on the first place. If accidentally civilians are killed, then the numbers of killed civilians should be much lower than those of soldiers. And this observation should be consistent for the entire siege period. So that was the starting point. The outcome of our analysis confirmed that in case of this episode of the siege of Sarajevo, the expectation has not been confirmed. There were many days in the siege when the numbers of killed civilians were much higher than the numbers of killed soldiers, or the same, or just little lower than the number of killed soldiers. So this finding is contrary to the initial expectation, and this is what we elaborated in the Karadzic report in the part related to timing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can have e-court page 18, and I believe we're on 65 ter 12130 already. Thank you. The top paragraph is what we'd like to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is the part of your report that regards timing, and I just have a couple questions for you in the top paragraph. Here you wrote about what you just termed as an assumption: "The reason for this is a simple belief [sic] that if civilians were not actively involved in fighting and stayed aside from it, one should expect that their deaths were accidental and unintended and thus must be proportionally lower than the number of killed soldiers." So is this what you meant when you talked about the assumption you had made?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did your support -- did your results support this assumption?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The results support the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have e-court page 28, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just below the box, you're talking your results. And you say that: [As read] "The above observations lead to the conclusion that two different processes were responsible for the victimisation of civilians and soldiers. One process was the driving force behind the killings and woundings of civilians, and another process stayed behind the killings and woundings of soldiers." Dr. Tabeau, what do you mean by here by "process"?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the process, I'm referring to in this paragraph is meant as the determining factors that were leading to killings of civilians and soldiers. The determining factors, of course, explicitly not -- are not studied here other than the study of causes of death, of course. Causes of death reported in this report which were discussed in the earlier sessions included shelling and sniping, other shooting, indirect causes related to war activities. These are expressions of these processes that were leading to death of civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And could these processes include military activity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Shelling and sniping doesn't occur by itself. It is, of course, combat activities, military activities, that are taking us -- leading us to the causes expressed as shelling, sniping, shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have e-court page 30. The top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here you speak about these results again. And you say: "Based on the results, ... the existence of the two different mechanisms driving the victimisation of civilians and soldiers has been confirmed. There is no reason to believe that killing and wounding of civilians was a direct consequence of, or related to, fighting of the armies involved in the combat in and around ... Sarajevo." So my question for you regards these mechanisms. You say that the existence of two different mechanisms. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these two different mechanisms -- if we say soldiers who are killed in combat activities, and this is this one mechanism, combat and fighting that kills the soldiers, the question is, What is the other mechanism that kills civilians? And if it is not combat and fighting, then it has to be targeting of civilians using means that are normally used for combat of armies. So what I'm trying to say is that in my opinion it has to be -- it had to be the targeting, intentional targeting of civilians that resulted in killing and wounding them in large numbers which are in many instances much, much higher, disproportionately higher, than numbers of killed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we could go to the handout, which 23719, and e-court page 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to talk about the numbers. Momentarily we will see a table. This is Table 8 taken from your report. And this regards the top 15 per cent of daily killings for soldiers. Can you tell us about this table?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table is a selection of data on killing of soldiers. This selection relates only to dates on which 15 per cent highest killings were noted. So it is if we would sort all the dates from these siege episode from the top number of killings of soldiers to the lowest number of killings of soldiers, then in this table it is only 15 per cent of the top dates with the highest numbers of killings of soldiers. Further, for this top 15 per cent, we report two variables: One is the number of killed civilians from all causes, and the second is the number of killed soldiers. And further, we calculate a ratio which is given in the second-last column in this table, CS ratio. This ratio expresses the number of killed soldiers in relation to the number of killed civilians. Its value for the first date, 2nd of May, 1992, is 6. That only means that per one civilian killed, there were six soldiers killed on this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so based on the assumption that you had when you first started this analysis that you told us about, that on days when there would be a high number of soldiers, there would be a less number of civilians, does this table support that assumption?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This expectation I mentioned initially only means that the CS ratio is higher than one. If it was one, the two numbers are exactly the same. If it is higher than one, and in -- the first row equals six, that means that soldiers were killed significantly more than civilians. So because in this table on all dates except for two, indicated with a "yes" in the last column, so for all other dates, the ratio is, indeed, higher than one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we can continue with that assumption, would one then expect to see, on the days with -- when most civilians were killed, even more soldiers killed?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is it correctly what we expect.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page of the handout, please, which is Table 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this table.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a similar table to the one we just discussed. The difference is that the selection of dates is made based on the number of killed civilians. This table represents the top 15 per cent of highest killings of civilians. And for this 15 per cent top daily killings, we calculated again the same measure, CS ratio, and in the last column of the table, with a "yes," I marked the values of the CS ratio, which are lower than one or just equal one. I think all are lower than one. This indicates that the number of killed civilians is higher than the number of killed soldiers, which is the opposite to what we have seen for soldiers for the top 15 per cent of killings of soldiers. It is the actually complete opposite of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what significance does that have for you in terms of the mechanisms that killed soldiers versus civilians?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is -- my initial result that makes me think these mechanisms must be different. These mechanisms are considerably different, which I further confirmed by several additional analysis summarised in the report in the section on timing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we just look below this table, what we see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions on the part ... The distinction of civilians and the soldiers was also coming from the two surveys, household surveys and the Bakije material. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This distinction that is presented in this table and analysed in the report comes from one source. The Household Survey Sarajevo. However, just to double-check that we were correct by using this distinction - the issue is, after all, of -- is essential, I think - we also compared the reporting of the civilian/military status in Sarajevo household survey with an alternative approach. The alternative being matching of the Sarajevo household survey with the military lists, and for all those marked, taking the military status from the military lists as the one observed, really. We further compared these two approaches, and in the second approach the number of civilians killed was slightly higher than in the first approach. So in order to be conservative, we decided to use the reporting from Sarajevo household survey. But I want to stress that a code -- a large per cent of records had the same coding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, what did you mean by "military list" when you said you matched the Sarajevo household survey with military lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Earlier today when discussing the sources, I reported that a number of additional sources were used, not for the list of victims itself, but for analysis like this one. The military lists were the lists I obtained from the ministries of defence of Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These are lists of those reported as killed in action or who went missing, being in the army. The lists covered three armies: The VRS, of course; ABiH army; and HVO army. So, in total, for the entire country, there is about 50.000 military casualties reported there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was waiting for the French translation. And as you -- as to your comment or conclusion that civilians were deliberately targeted, in relation to that I wonder whether the fact that there are many civilians victims would necessarily lead to such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not only the fact that there were that many civilian victims in relation to military casualties on the same dates, it is not only this reason that led me to draw this conclusion. I studied the similarity between the timing of killing of civilians and soldiers statistically and the same I have done for wounding. I calculated several statistical measures of the similarity of these two different distributions and consistently my result was that these two patterns are statistically different and significantly so. That is one type. I also studied other techniques to confirm one -- the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted - please correct me if I'm wrong - that more people died because of shelling than because of sniping or shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is probably right. If we go back to the table on causes of death, then we can verify this conclusion. But, of course, it is a right conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then does the location of the army have any impact or effect on such result if the -- for example, if an army is located in the middle of civilian population. Does it have any effect on that, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I believe it does matter where the army is located. Absolutely. Yeah. For shelling, there is a separate analysis in the report. And I compared the victims of shelling for both civilians and soldiers, and the conclusion is not different for this particular category. So these are two different patterns, I think. As for the location of the army, the VRS was located, of course, on the hills with an excellent view on the town down the valley, so I think it was a perfect location for shelling of any victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please proceed. I take it you have been to Sarajevo several times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been many times to Sarajevo and had the opportunity to walk along the actual front lines on the hills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we go to the bottom of this page, there's another figure below this table. This looks -- it's a chart, it's a visualisation. Can you just tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a selection of days from this episode of the siege. In total there were 162 days in this episode. On this chart, 51 days are shown. These are the days on which the number of killed civilians was higher than the number of killed soldiers. It is a larger per cent of the overall number of days, 31.5 per cent of days, for which this observation holds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this issue of timing, did you make this same analysis in your second and third report about Sarajevo as well?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We'll eventually get there, but now we're going to -- we'll move to the second report, which is the Galic report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 12131.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this report picks up the timing -- the time-period where the Karadzic report leaves off; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what area does this report -- what geographical area does it cover?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is exactly the same area within the front lines area in Sarajevo. And the same source is used for this report exactly as for the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So you answered my next question. The household survey was used for this report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And the results you obtained for the Galic report, are those similar to the Karadzic report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the numbers are higher compared with the first episode, because the episode itself is longer than the first one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right. And for the Galic report, the episode is almost about two years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can -- sorry to keep going back and forth, but may I have the handout again, and now we're looking at page 10, which is e-court page 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to review some tables for Galic, and this is going to be quite similar to what we did in Karadzic -- the Karadzic report. So at first we will look at Table 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we need the handout which is 65 ter 23719, please. E-court page 11. I think everybody has the handout itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we have Table 1 in front of us. Can you tell us what this table is?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same table as already shown for the first episode in the Karadzic report. Here, the numbers are higher. The number of killed persons is 3.798. And the number of wounded persons is 12.919. Further down in the table, we include basic distributions by sex, age, civilian/military status, and, of course, cause of killing and wounding.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question. As to the distinction between civilian and soldiers, what are the examples of unknown status? Does it mean that they didn't answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly the meaning: no answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And under "status" in this table, we see civilians killed, 1.399; civilians wounded, 5.093. And then we go to the table below it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is this where we deal specifically with civilians?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is civilians only. Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And is this separated in the same manner?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can turn the page to page 11. Again we see another table with which we're familiar. This regards killed, cause of death, wounded, cause of wounding. Let's work on Table 6, the section up top that involves fire-arms. If we add all those totals up --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are very high totals for fire-arms. For killings, it is 89.2 per cent; and for wounding, the fire-arms are responsible for 95.4 per cent of all wounding cases. The remaining causes have much less significance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we turn the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- can we stay there. Second group in the causes of death among direct casualties of war, and I see "human shield, 4." How do we come to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no -- my conclusion here, it is the data as reported by the respondents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So they responded they -- certain individuals died as human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the meaning, I understand, of this response. There is very little affect of my work here. As I said, it was for me to clean it up a little bit and regroup and present in a table. It is not that I am recording the human shields from something else to human shields. It is not what I have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if I can pick up on that. May we go to 65 ter 12130.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I just want to go back to the Karadzic report for just one moment, and we're going to look at the annex, and the reason being is the annex includes the actual questionnaire that was used in the household survey.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So 65 ter 12130. May I have the ERN ending in 8506, please. I think it's probably page 40.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This the English translation of the questionnaire. And you mentioned that you were specifically interested in killed and wounded, and I see here that's 5 and 6. Tell us about this information that was asked.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we can see for killed persons, and the same is later for wounded - I'm talking about question 5 - so information collected about those killed included names of these individuals, year of birth, position in the household, date of death, place of death, cause of death, and the civilian/military status. So all these items were collected explicitly reported on the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So when you received information in your tables, for example, the direct casualties of war, and it was listed - we just saw it a second ago - cold steel, slaughtered, tortured, for example, execution, human shield, disappeared - is that information that is specifically coming from this questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is coming from the responses to these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that was the questionnaire in the Karadzic case. That was the same questionnaire used for the Galic case as well?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same questionnaire and the same source.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to the handout, please, to page 12 of the handout, and we'll continue on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now we spoke earlier about the statistical formula of capture/recapture, and I don't want to talk about that again, because we'll talk about it next time, but I do want to talk about the results that came from that formula in the Galic case. And up top we see Table 18. Can you tell us about the numbers you found for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It should be next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us about these results in this two-year period of time.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are results in Table 18 of the capture/recapture method, exactly the same method and the same sources as were applied in the Karadzic report. The information reported here includes the estimated number for all ethnic groups, including Muslims, with the number 3.437. This was produced as the initial estimate in the first step of the estimation and extrapolated, in the next phases, exactly the same way as it was done for Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so for here we see, under "Muslims," the surveyed during that period of time reported 2.340. And then what was the estimate?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The estimate is 4.352 for all ethnic groups. The number 2.963 is lower than what we have seen in Table 1 because, here, only records linked are shown. That makes for the difference, makes up for the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it is exactly the same data we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you say "linked," linked from what to what?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, in the Galic report, the links between Sarajevo household survey and the Bakije funeral home, the links go to the population census. The matched records listed here are those matched with the population census and therefore are lower than the overall numbers presented in Table 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, we're going to move on to timing. And you mentioned that you did the same timing analysis in the Galic report that you did in the Karadzic report. And let's look here at Table 13. Tell us what this table reports.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Table 13 reports on killed civilians and soldiers for days when only -- when six or more civilians were killed. This table relates only to one year of the two studied. It's just a selection from the second year. There is another table in the report for the first year so that the analysis is complete. So also in this table, when we go through the numbers of killed civilians and soldiers, we see that for all but two dates the civilians are killed in higher numbers than soldiers. And the same is observed for the days selection of high days from the first year of the siege in the table in the report similar as this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. When go to Table 14, days when even more civilians were killed, 20 civilians or more were killed, what you did -- excuse me, wounded.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What did you find?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is again a table related to very high days, 20 civilians wounded on one day, it's a lot, so, again, the same pattern. The numbers of wounded civilians much, much higher than the number of wounded soldiers. The same is in the report for the first period.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what are the significance of these figures to you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these figures confirm the conclusion I already presented for the first episode of the siege discussed in the Karadzic report. I think my conclusion also holds for this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like now to move to the third Sarajevo report. 65 ter 12135. And this is the -- a report for when Dragomir Milosevic was the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What's the time-frame of this report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report comprises events from the last year of the siege, August 1994 to November 1995. The final, final stages of the war. Yes. And the area, similar but not identical to the previous reports. This report is compiled using actually different sources. The same methodology. But because of the different sources, the area is also slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the core of it remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So this report uses the same methodology; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Why did you use different sources?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the obvious difficulty that Sarajevo household survey actually ended with reports for August/September 1994 and there is no more data in it. So what I studied in Dragomir is not covered in the Sarajevo household survey.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What sources did you use?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sources are different than Household Survey Sarajevo but also very reliable and made by professional statisticians. I used two -- the so-called DEM-2 databases, one of Republika Srpska and one of the Federation. These DEM-2 databases are called so because they are electronic expression of what is reported to statistical authority on the so-called DEM-2 form. This is a form that is used in official death notifications that citizens are obliged to make in case of death in their family to statistical authority. So these were my major sources --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor for record, could you spell them two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: D-E-M-2, like a number, 2, DEM-2. It is -- the "dem" comes from "demographic" death notification form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And these databases, you had one from the RS and one from the Federation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. These databases were based, as I said, on official death notifications from the war time. All together for the entire country these databases comprised 140.000 records, cases, death cases. Information collected by the authorities and processed here included both war-related violent deaths and also natural deaths. We actually requested the information about natural deaths in order to be able to exclude it from further analysis. But if we would not have it, it would be to make sure that we worked with categories that are not mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. What other sources did you use?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third source. In addition to these two, was the ICRC list of missing persons. ICRC is International Committee for Red Cross. They are mandated to trace missing persons in case of conflict and war. I included the list of missing persons by ICRC because missing persons are not reported in official death notifications. It is impossible because death certificate don't exist for these kind of cases. And secondly, I choice ICRC for its quality. A very well-known, high quality of information. So these three sources were the basic sources for compiling the list of victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now let's talk about your sources for your wounded numbers. What were those sources?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wounded persons are taken their records from Sarajevo hospital records. I was able to use records from three hospitals in Sarajevo. This is not all hospital records available for this period. There were more hospitals. There were two war hospitals in Sarajevo. And emergency health stations, these records are not used. So the three hospitals that I used are actually a small sample of all information about wounding process. It's a very small, limited sample, but it's a very good sample because, first of all, the selection concentrated on civilians. All men at age 18 to, I think, 65, were excluded. They are not reported in the sample. Only persons below age 18 and women are included. Yet it is a small number that was collected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. That's the amount of time you should put a pause. French translation is just now completed. Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd now like to talk about the methodology you used in getting the numbers for the killings.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in the reports - for the parties - this starts at page 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us what your first step was when you looked at all these sources and had to put it together.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what we always do in the beginning, we study each source, assess it, clean it up a little bit, exclude duplications, and match it with the population census. We have done this with all our sources on victims. In the second step, we integrated the sources of -- on victims in one large data table.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So when you talk about integration, does that mean you merged the DEM-2 databases and ICRC lists?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the meaning of it. Merging is increasing the number of cases by putting one source on the top of the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the next step?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one more thing. So these three sources, DEM-2 databases, ICRC lists, is the core, the most important source, as such, for the Dragomir Milosevic report, but because the whole database was established for actually entire country, so in addition to these three, we also included Sarajevo household survey and Bakije funeral home for earlier periods, not those who were later analysed in Dragomir. Just clarification. But it doesn't change the nature of the data used for Dragomir. So having merged all these lists, the next step is to identify the overlap of the lists. The overlap means that records of the same persons are repeated in several sources. As we can easily imagine, they are repeated in DEM-2 databases, especially the Federation part of it, and the Sarajevo household survey. Moreover, we already know that household survey Sarajevo overlaps quite well with Bakije funeral home. So there is a lot of overlap in this merge of lists. But, of course, we are able -- we know -- we have techniques that can be done to identify the overlap and eliminate all records that would duplicate information about victims. So that is what we have done in this phase.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So at this point you have a large database for the entire country for the entire war period; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in order to focus solely on the Dragomir Milosevic time-period and the geographical area of Sarajevo, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to be able to -- to focus on this area, we had to extract a portion of this database, the portion related to Sarajevo, and for this portion, eliminate any duplicated information, specifically for this part, to end with a reasonable list, reliable list, from which we could extract relevant records for the report for the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the correct time-period and the correct area, how many records did you have?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 26.000 records. These twenty-six -- specifically 26.466, this number covers the entire war period, meaning April ninety -- even January 1992 to December 1995, and, actually, not six, but ten Sarajevo municipalities. The ten Sarajevo municipalities comprise the six urban municipalities exactly the same as studied in the Galic report and Karadzic report, plus four extra municipalities. This is a broad selection, but we don't make these kind of databases every day, and there might be always questions that are broader than just the report that we are making. So the idea of making this kind of database as the basis is actually related to these additional questions that may come up in the future. But having this database, we have selected from it only the relevant records according to time and area criteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So now we have a database that regards this time-frame, this area. Does that database differentiate between soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In DEM-2 databases and in the ICRC list, there is no information about civilian/military status. So it was not possible for us to take it as reported in our original sources and process it into statistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, in this case, used the military lists that I mentioned earlier today and cross-referenced these lists by matching, individual-level matching, with the records in the Sarajevo database.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you found any reporting that an individual was a soldier, even if that was inconsistent with other reporting, how did you count that person?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first step we just marked all those confirmed on military lists as soldiers. That was step number one. And, further, we have also Sarajevo household survey in this database. So for a number of records, we can compare further the information obtained from the military lists with the actual reporting in the Sarajevo household survey. So for many records, the information was consistent. Actually, for majority of records. For a small number of records, there was a different reporting of individuals. So we again opted for the conservative approach, that we coded as soldiers everybody ever reported as soldier in any source.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can turn to the handout and go to page 13. This is Table 6 on top. It regards an estimate of military status.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, can you tell us about this table, please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table relates to the entire Sarajevo database. We see the overall total of individuals included here listed in the last row as 26.466. That is the general Sarajevo database, entire war period. Above this number, there is a distribution of it into civilians, militaries, or soldiers, and there is a category called unknown. What interests us at this stage is the category called unknown. This is the number of cases for which we did not have any information from our matching with military lists. But we don't want, of course, to have a large number of unknown status because it -- it hampers a good analysis of this data. And moreover, for a large number of the unknowns, a good information was available from Sarajevo household survey. So we go back to Sarajevo household survey and check how these unknowns are reported there, and obviously we find two components listed in this table under the column "correction." 1.715 are those who were reported civilians. So we take them and record them into civilians. And they are gone from the unknowns. And we go and look for soldiers among the unknowns, and we see 886 reported as soldiers in Sarajevo household survey. So we record these cases as soldiers. So they are gone from unknowns and moved to soldiers. This is one type of correction: Improving of the unknowns. But, as I say, we always compare, always cross-reference information if we have it. So when we compared the coding of the status between Sarajevo household survey and military records, we saw a small number, 608, 608, that were actually civilians in our first approach but soldiers in Sarajevo household survey. In order not to inflate the number of civilians, we recorded them into soldiers because this number was reported inconsistently between these two sources, and we don't want to keep the number of civilians high. We want to keep it low, as low as possible, because we want to be conservative. We don't want to make numbers higher than they should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we go to the column entitled "final number," we can see that you've altered your figures, but we still see a number in the unknown table.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For this number, there is nothing we can do. And this is the cases that will stay like that, that we can only hope that the number of unknowns in the Dragomir Milosevic case area and time span will be low. We will see in a second, in the second table, how really high it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So let's move down to Table 11. And we have two tables, and let's start on the left. Can you tell us about this table?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To comment on the number of records with unknown civilian/military status, in total there were 571 such records related to the Dragomir Milosevic case area and time span. This number is mentioned in the table -- in the left table, at the bottom, under "unknown status" --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And just stop there are for a moment. That number, 571, is different than in Table 6, the unknown, 3454; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Because --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Why was it different? It is, in Table 11 we actually made one extra step between Table 6 and 11. In Table 11, instead of the entire database, we talk about a selection of cases from the Sarajevo database, the selection that relates to the Dragomir Milosevic case. Except, of course, for cases of natural deaths which are also included. And in a second I will explain how they were excluded. But for the time being, we have to take a note of the fact that we extracted records, and speak of Dragomir Milosevic cases only.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So Table 11 regards only the Dragomir Milosevic time-frame; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So continue on explaining Table 11.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second issue that needed to be sorted out next to the unknown civilian/military status was the unknown cause of killing, of death. In our databases, there are two parallel reports on causes of death. One is the reporting of medical causes of death. There is an example in the report of medical causes. I think it is ... it is Table 12 on page 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So medical causes include, for examples, injury, all kinds of -- different types of injuries, like crushing injuries, other injuries, open-head wounds, neck fractures. Well, the cause of death is expressed as a medical category. A list of the causes is included in 12 -- in Table 12 on page 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you could stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is page 26 of 65 ter 12135 and we won't go there. And it's a number of causes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But tell us the source of these causes. Where did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These causes are reported in DEM-2 databases. The large databases, they were the core sources for this report. But, as I said, parallel to the medical causes of death, there is another way of reporting of causes of death. There's another way indicated explicitly whether a death case is a war-related violent death or not. For us, for our purposes, this information is essential, because we are not looking for all available medical causes, disregarding how relevant they might be to our cases, it is important for us to make sure that we extract violent war-related deaths for this analysis. And in Table 11, the left part of the table, we can read that there were 981 cases of violent war-related causes. 981 is the total of violent war-related deaths. This number, 981, is an absolute minimum of the cases that we consider to be the victims related to the last episode of the siege, the one related to Dragomir Milosevic report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And, now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just can you go back, can we see the page, Table 12, medical causes of violent war-related deaths.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That is 65 ter 12135, e-court page 26, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the page ending with 6397? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, did you have a question on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, just one question. I -- I found some strange cause of deaths; for example, number 53, toxic effect of alcohol. And number 49, poisoning by diuretics and other unspecified drugs, medicaments, and biological substances. How are they related to violent war-related death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in this table, the causes are presented as reported in the DEM-2 databases. For these two cases, we also have an indication that these causes were -- these two cases were related to war. They were war -- indicated as war victims. Well, how they could be related to war victims? Obviously poisoning is not the same as shooting, shelling, or sniping. Obviously it is a completely different category of cause of death. This category, this cause of death, I can imagine would be easily possible in a territory under siege and wouldn't be listed under causes like shelling or sniping or other shooting but would be listed in a separate category which we also had in Sarajevo -- in the two previous Sarajevo reports as indirect, for instance, cases of war deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we go back to the handout, page 13 of the handout, and go on the table from the left side, where we see numbers in green, to the table on the right side where we don't see numbers in the green unknown section, can you just tell us in a very brief --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- general way how you redistributed those numbers --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- and what the basis for that was?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The green areas contain unknowns on both civilian/military status and on cause of death. About the unknowns, we assumed that they contained both categories: war-related victims, and natural deaths. So what we did, we statistically distributed the unknowns proportionally to the observed distribution highlighted in the -- I don't know, yellowish colour, something like that. I don't know exactly how to call this other colour in the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this was a distribution by proportion?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the allocation of unknowns among the two types of well-defined categories using the proportionality assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Turn the page in the handout. We're now going to move to wounded. Tell us about the source of the information for this table.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table is based on hospital records. It includes all the records reported in the three hospitals. These are cases of hospitalised wounded persons only. The total of cases for the entire siege period is 3.036. Of those, we identified 405 listed in the last row of the table as the cases of hospitalised wounded persons related to the Dragomir Milosevic case. It is, again, by selecting according to the time criterion. Area of all cases is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So this number is based on actual observed numbers, correct, this is a minimum number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a very, very low absolute minimum number.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to turn -- to skip a page in the handout and go directly to page 16 and talk about timing in the Milosevic case. Did you do the same analysis here that you had done in Karadzic and Galic?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Timing was analysed exactly the same way as it was in the first and second report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And in those reports we saw different types of tables, and here again is a third type of table. And this regards numbers of deaths per day. Please tell us about this.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this table gives a summary of what we observed on the so-called low days and high days, just a summary, not listed here day by day, but just summary of numbers of killed civilians and soldiers on low and high days. Low days are those when one to two deaths per day were observed. High days are days with three or more deaths per day were observed. If we move to the second column of the table, then we see the number of days. How many were there in the siege? There were 224 days that can be considered low, and 107 that can be considered high. Out of a total of 487. 487, for transcript. On the low days, the number of killed civilians was, in total, 160; and soldiers, 102; 46 were unknowns. The number of civilians, as we see, is considerably higher than the number of killed soldiers. On the high days, the number of killed civilians is 289; and of soldiers, 317. The number of killed civilians is lower - not considerably, though - than the number of killed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Doctor, what conclusion did you come to based on those numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion is exactly the same and [sic] in the two previous reports, but I want to note that conclusion is drawn on many more analysis than what we just seen in this table. This table is a small selection of all ways of analysis that is completed and presented in the report. So the conclusion is that the mechanisms killing civilians and soldiers are different, and significantly so, and civilians must have been targeted specifically because their numbers are so high on many, many days in every episode of the siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 12135, page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to the bottom of the page. This is your Milosevic report. In the last paragraph, you noted, in talking about this timing, that: "The above findings suggest that the civilian population of Sarajevo had systematically been the target for military attacks disregarding the actual presence of heavy combat activity [sic]. This also indicates that a targeted terror campaign against civilians likely continued for most of the period from August of 1994 to November of 1995." Dr. Tabeau, can you explain to us how your analysis supports a targeted terror campaign in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- the basis for this conclusion is the significant difference between the timing of killings of civilians and soldiers and of wounding of civilians and soldiers. On many days in every episode, numbers of killed civilians were higher than the number of killed soldiers. If the mechanism would have been the same and it would be combat, killing both, this observation would not hold. So the mechanism killing civilians must have been related to targeting them, disregarding of combat activities going on in the siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to move on to the Srebrenica reports. I wonder if you would like me to do that or is this the time to stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to suggest to you to stop for today here. In addition, there are a couple of matters I'd like to deal with. And I was also informed that Mr. Karadzic has something to raise. Shall we excuse the witness? Or ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we are getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for what the witness would like to raise, I would like the witness to be present. I can repeat it. So regarding the issue that I would like to raise, I would like Dr. Tabeau to be present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to inform you that Dr. Tabeau was kind and agreed to meet the Defence, and we agreed that all scientific findings, hers, as in any scientific study, can be tested and repeated if they are checked using -- applying the same methods and using the same materials, so I would appreciate it if Dr. Tabeau could provide us during the day today or tomorrow all the materials that she used. Especially the census for 1996 that Dr. Tabeau rejected. Then 1997 and 1998 census materials. I would also like to have the ethnic composition of the authorities, the organ in power in -- the government organs in 1996, 1997, and 1998, as elected after the elections. I would also like - and I'm not sure if I have that - a census from 1991 with all the relevant names, the address, father's name, and the JMBG number. I would also like Dr. Tabeau to kindly forward to us the techniques and the tools and procedures that she used and that she meant a moment ago that she -- that she mentioned a moment ago that she applied in eliminating duplicates. She probably did mention them, but we do not have them in the reports. We would also appreciate getting information of displaced persons and refugees for the entire country and especially according to their ethnic structure. Also, information on the dead and missing for the entire territory of the country, and especially in reference to what Dr. Tabeau said on page 89, to obtain the analysis that were used to get the information that were entered in the last table that were used and that were not included in the report. I would appreciate receiving this so that I can prepare for my cross-examination over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I hear from you, Dr. Tabeau, I will ask you, Mr. Karadzic, why could you not have requested such request on your own? Why only now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I did not know how these results would be presented and what the conclusions would be that she would mention in the examination-in-chief. So it is obvious that I will have to repeat all these processes and -- because I would like to test them and see what the results would be that we would obtain. Also, in view of the general context, it turns out now that it is necessary to request this information because I've just learned that the 1996 census was rejected, although it is immediately following the war, as opposed to 1997 and 1998. And also I realise that there was information that needs to be tested and checked by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, you must have received all of her reports a long time ago. But, very well. Do you have any observation, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My observation is just that, Your Honour. It is quite late in the game to be asking for this material. It's certainly material that the defendant himself should have used to come to his own conclusions. The main basis of all of these reports are the 1991 census and the voters' registration from 1997 and 1998. Those he had received. I do note that he just said something about a 1996 census. It must be a mistranslation. It must be something other than a census, because there wasn't one. But nonetheless, anything that happened in 1996 doesn't now make his request in 2012 more relevant today than it could have been two years ago. In addition to the matching criteria that he asked for, that is in the report. There's nothing new that he is asking for that he has not had this whole entire time. And finally, the Karadzic report on municipalities which was provided in, I believe, 2009 is the exact same methodology and sources that are in the Galic report. There is nothing new being done here. The most recent report that he was given - we'll get to this - is the Srebrenica report, and that was recently, because Dr. Tabeau did it off the recent ICMP database information. But again, that's just additional numbers. That has nothing to do with methodology or sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the previous session you said you would come back to us as to the flagged material, 1991 census, as regards counting of displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're trying to do that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction. I did not say the census from 1996 but, rather, the voters' lists of 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I know I was overlapping. That's a separate matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, do you have any observation with respect to Mr. Karadzic's request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, first of all, I am aware of the practice of the OTP from many other cases when it comes to disclosure of sources used for demographic and other reports. All sources, I'm sure, I used in my reports have been disclosed by the OTP, and I can imagine long time ago. So the population census of 1991; the voters' registers, 1997/1998; the military lists. Further, Sarajevo household survey, Bakije funeral home, DEM-2 databases. I'm sure it all has been disclosed. It is impossible that it is otherwise. So that is one point. It is the practice, in scientific research, to disclose the sources. And when the methods are described, it is possible for anybody else to redo the analysis using the same data. So I think in order to challenge what I have done, Mr. Karadzic has all he needs for this. And it is very naive to believe that this work can be redone over the weekend. This is my conclusion. We are speaking of millions and millions of records that have to -- have been analysed. Overdoing this in one weekend, in three days, even though it is a long weekend, I don't think is feasible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, briefly, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, simply, we will take a random sample and test the data. On the other hand, I'm not certain that I received all the information for the entire country, and that would be absolutely necessary because this was a closed system, it had very hard borders, and it was difficult to leave the country. So the fluctuation of the population within the country was huge, and I would need to have all this information related to Muslims for the entire country and not just for the nine or 27 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard the parties and Dr. Tabeau, the Chamber would leave it at that and, if necessary, that may be a subject of separate litigation. I'll note the time, but given that we started a bit later today, I think I have time to issue a couple of oral rulings. First the Chamber will issue an oral decision on the accused's motion for public admission of exhibits under seal filed confidentially on 10th of April, 2012. In the motion, the accused requests that the Chamber reassign a new exhibit number to all exhibits admitted under seal in this case except for witness statements and plea agreements and admit them publicly in order for the parties and the Chamber to refer to them in public filings and in the final judgement without them being associated with a particular witness. The Prosecution filed its response on the 19th of April, 2012, requesting that the Chamber dismiss the accused's motion on the basis that the accused fails to identify any specific confidential exhibit which should be made public and to substantiate his request for reconsideration of all the Chamber's decisions to admit exhibits confidentially, and, finally, because his suggested approach is unworkable and ineffective. The Chamber first recalls that in balancing the importance of conducting a public trial while protecting the identity of witnesses and victims, the Chamber has exercised utmost caution in determining whether to place exhibits under seal throughout the trial. The Chamber further recalls countless examples where it has inquired proprio motu about the necessity of placing an exhibit under seal, and, whenever possible, the Chamber has ordered the parties to produce public redacted versions of exhibits placed under seal. Moreover, the Chamber recalls that in the motion, the accused has not provided any specific examples of exhibits admitted under seal which it argues should be made public. In this respect, the Chamber considers the accused's request to be vague and unsubstantiated, bordering on frivolous, and the Chamber will not engage in a review of each of its decisions to admit exhibits under seal in this case. The accused's motion is therefore denied. Next, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the accused's request filed yesterday to admit into evidence the public and under seal versions of KDZ612's supplemental statement now that the required attestation under Rule 92 bis (B) has been provided. Having reviewed the under seal version of the supplemental statement which has been uploaded into e-court as 1D5557, the Chamber is satisfied that the certification procedure fulfils the formal requirements of Rule 92 bis (B). The Chamber therefore requests the Registry to record the confidential version of KDZ612's supplemental statement is admitted into evidence and to assign an exhibit number to it. In relation to the public redacted version of KDZ612's supplemental statement which has been uploaded into e-court as 1D5558, the Chamber notes that the Rule 92 bis attestation has not been attached to it. The Chamber therefore requests the accused to attach a redacted version of the 92 bis attestation to the document currently uploaded as 1D5558. The Chamber further instructs the Registry to assign an exhibit number to this document and to record that it is admitted into evidence. Doctor, we'll resume next week on --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- on Tuesday at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I just, in transcript, small intervention in transcript. I said: Not only for the Muslims and not only for 27 municipalities. In transcript, it is concerning only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's noted. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of May, 2012, at 11.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.06 p.m.,
